Benchmarking short-read splicing classification against long-read ground truth

Author

Benjamin Fair

Published

August 25, 2026

What this notebook does

It rebuilds the key figures of the simulation benchmark, reading only the small plot-ready files in output/ — so it runs in seconds and needs none of the pipeline’s intermediates.

Almost everything here descends from one table, output/master_confusion_table.tsv.gz (78 KB), which the Snakemake workflow reduces from roughly 350 GB of alignments and clustering output. That table is shipped with the project, so the figures reproduce without running anything.

Note

The workflow reproduces the shipped table closely but not exactly, because it calls a newer leafcutter2 than the one that produced the published classifications. The differences are measured in FOOTNOTES.md; every metric’s median change is zero.

The benchmark, for a new reader

The problem. A splicing classifier has to decide, for each splice junction seen in short-read RNA-seq, whether it belongs to a productive transcript or an unproductive one (destined for nonsense-mediated decay). This is easy when the junction is annotated and hard when it isn’t — and unannotated junctions are exactly where unproductive splicing hides. So a benchmark needs ground truth for junctions that no annotation contains, which an annotation-derived truth set cannot provide.

The trick. Simulate the short reads from real full-length long-read cDNAs. Each of the 334,430 long reads was translated and classified productive/unproductive by NMDFinderB from the full-length molecule, independent of any annotation. Short reads are then simulated from those same molecules. So every junction — annotated or not — carries a truth label, and the classifier’s job is to recover it from fragments.

What is varied. Four axes, crossed:

Axis Levels
Sequencing depth 7, from 20 GB (~100 M read pairs) down to 1/64 of that
3’ coverage bias 5 Beta(alpha, 1) fragment-bias conditions, uniform → extreme (a proxy for degraded RNA / low RIN)
Annotation given to the classifier comprehensive Gencode; minimal (MANE); minimal but with complete ORF ends (MinOrfEnds)
Classification method 4, below

The four methods. Two annotation baselines and two readings of leafcutter2:

Method Rule
Annotations believe the GTF; decline to call anything unannotated
Assume unannotated is UP believe the GTF; call anything unannotated unproductive
Leaf2 junction_classifier leafcutter2’s raw Coding flag alone — an intermediate signal, taken without annotation or UTR context. Never declines.
Leaf2 multi-flag leafcutter2’s actual final PR/UP/NE verdict — the label the tool appends to intron names in its clustered output

The last two are not “the tool” versus “a custom rule”: they are the tool’s internal coding flag versus the tool’s published classification. Comparing them measures what leafcutter2’s consolidation logic buys over the bare flag.

Junction subclasses. Every junction carries three bits, GencodePC:Annot:UTR — is it in a Gencode protein-coding transcript, is it annotated at all, does it lie in a UTR. These are always assigned from comprehensive Gencode, even when scoring the MANE or MinOrfEnds runs, so a subclass means the same thing in every panel. 0:0:* is the interesting corner: junctions no annotation knows about.

The master confusion table

# Source data: one entry per panel, collected as the notebook runs and written to a single
# multi-tab spreadsheet (one tab per panel, main and supplemental together) at the end.
SOURCE_DATA = {}


def record_source(panel, df):
    """Stash the exact table behind a panel's plot, keyed by its panel label."""
    assert panel not in SOURCE_DATA, f"duplicate source-data panel label: {panel}"
    SOURCE_DATA[panel] = df.reset_index(drop=True).copy()


master = pd.read_csv(OUTPUT / "master_confusion_table.tsv.gz", sep="\t")
for col in COUNT_COLS:
    master[col] = master[col].fillna(0)
master["Subclass"] = pd.Categorical(
    master["Subclass"], categories=SUBCLASS_LEVELS, ordered=True)

print(f"{len(master):,} rows x {master.shape[1]} columns")
print(f"{master.GTF.nunique()} annotation sets"
      f" x {master.Method.nunique()} methods"
      f" x {master.Subclass.nunique()} subclasses"
      f" x {master.Coverage_GB.nunique()} depths"
      f" x {master.Coverage_bias_Beta_params.nunique()} bias conditions")
1,512 rows x 19 columns
3 annotation sets x 4 methods x 7 subclasses x 7 depths x 5 bias conditions

One row per (annotation set, method, subclass, depth, bias condition). The eight count columns partition every ground-truth junction:

Column Meaning
TP truly unproductive, called unproductive
TN truly productive, called productive
FP truly productive, called unproductive
FN truly unproductive, called productive
UP_NE_ByMethod truly unproductive, but the method declined to call it
PR_NE_ByMethod truly productive, but the method declined to call it
UP_NotDetected truly unproductive, junction not seen in the short reads at this depth
PR_NotDetected truly productive, not seen at this depth

The last four columns are what make this more than a confusion matrix. A method that refuses to answer, and a depth too shallow to see the junction, are different kinds of failure from a wrong answer — and both have to be charged somewhere, or an abstaining method looks artificially good.

That is why there are two recalls. Recall_v1 is TP / (TP + FN), which scores only the junctions a method actually called. Recall_v2 is TP / (TP + FN + UP_NE_ByMethod + UP_NotDetected), which scores against every ground-truth unproductive junction, so declining to answer and failing to detect both count as misses. Recall_v2 is the honest number, and the one used below.

Code 
metrics = master.copy()
metrics["n_classified"] = metrics[["TP", "TN", "FP", "FN"]].sum(axis=1)
metrics["Accuracy"] = np.where(
    metrics.n_classified > 0,
    (metrics.TP + metrics.TN) / metrics.n_classified, np.nan)
metrics["Precision"] = np.where(
    (metrics.TP + metrics.FP) > 0, metrics.TP / (metrics.TP + metrics.FP), np.nan)
metrics["Recall_v1"] = np.where(
    (metrics.TP + metrics.FN) > 0, metrics.TP / (metrics.TP + metrics.FN), np.nan)
metrics["Recall_v2"] = metrics.TP / (
    metrics.TP + metrics.FN + metrics.UP_NE_ByMethod + metrics.UP_NotDetected)
metrics["FPR_v2"] = metrics.FP / (
    metrics.FP + metrics.TN + metrics.PR_NE_ByMethod + metrics.PR_NotDetected)
metrics["Method_long"] = pd.Categorical(
    metrics.Method.map(METHOD_LONG), categories=METHOD_LONG_LEVELS, ordered=True)

FigS4C — junction subclass composition and ground-truth productivity

As published: junctions binned by leafcutter2’s full 4-bit flag (GencodePC:Annot:Coding:UTR, packed as 8*GencodePC + 4*Annot + 2*Coding + 1*UTR), at the reference condition (comprehensive Gencode, 20 GB, uniform coverage). Only 12 of the 16 possible combinations are populated — GencodePC=1 with Annot=0 (decimal flags 8-11) essentially never happens, since a junction Gencode calls part of a productive isoform is (trivially) also one it annotates at all. Bar colour is the Leaf2 multi-flag verdict for that exact flag combination (a deterministic lookup on the decimal flag, independent of any particular junction): {0, 4} -> UP, {1, 5} -> NE, everything else -> PR.

Unannotated junctions (decimal flags 0-3, GencodePC=Annot=0) split close to evenly between productive and unproductive, while fully annotated ones (12-15) are overwhelmingly productive — the imbalance an annotation-blind classifier has to overcome.

FigS4D — classification accuracy by method and junction subclass

The same reference condition as FigS4C, now crossing all four classification methods. Annotation-only methods score NaN on the two unannotated subclasses — they have nothing to say about a junction no annotation contains — which is exactly the gap the two leafcutter2 methods fill.

Code 
ref_d = pd.concat([
    master[master.GTF.eq("Comprehensive_Gencode") & master.Coverage_GB.eq(20)
           & master.Coverage_bias_Beta_params.eq("alpha_1_beta_1")],
    master[master.GTF.eq("Comprehensive_Gencode") & master.Coverage_GB.isna()],
], ignore_index=True)
ref_d = ref_d[ref_d.Subclass.isin(SUBCLASS_LEVELS[:-1])].copy()
ref_d["n_classified"] = ref_d[["TP", "TN", "FP", "FN"]].sum(axis=1)
ref_d["Accuracy"] = np.where(ref_d.n_classified > 0,
                             (ref_d.TP + ref_d.TN) / ref_d.n_classified, np.nan)

METHOD_D_ORDER = ["Annotations", "Assume unannotated is UP",
                  "Leaf2 junction_classifier", "Leaf2 multi-flag"]
piv_acc = (ref_d.pivot(index="Method", columns="Subclass", values="Accuracy")
           .reindex(index=METHOD_D_ORDER, columns=SUBCLASS_LEVELS[:-1]) * 100)
piv_n = (ref_d.pivot(index="Method", columns="Subclass", values="n_classified")
         .reindex(index=METHOD_D_ORDER, columns=SUBCLASS_LEVELS[:-1]))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 2.4))
im = ax.imshow(np.ma.masked_invalid(piv_acc.to_numpy()), cmap="viridis",
              vmin=0, vmax=100, aspect="auto")
for i in range(piv_acc.shape[0]):
    for j in range(piv_acc.shape[1]):
        v, n = piv_acc.iloc[i, j], piv_n.iloc[i, j]
        lab = "" if np.isnan(v) else f"{v:.1f}\n(n={int(n):,})"
        ax.text(j, i, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6, color="white")
ax.set_xticks(range(len(SUBCLASS_LEVELS[:-1])))
ax.set_xticklabels(SUBCLASS_LEVELS[:-1], fontsize=8)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(METHOD_D_ORDER)))
ax.set_yticklabels(METHOD_D_ORDER, fontsize=7)
ax.set_xlabel("Junction subclass, GencodePC:Annot:UTR", fontsize=8)
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.04, pad=0.02).set_label("Accuracy (%)", fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()


def correct_incorrect(method, subclass):
    r = ref_d[(ref_d.Method == method) & (ref_d.Subclass == subclass)].iloc[0]
    return r.TP + r.TN, r.FP + r.FN


from scipy.stats import chi2_contingency
for m1, m2, sub in [("Assume unannotated is UP", "Leaf2 multi-flag", "0:0:0"),
                    ("Leaf2 junction_classifier", "Leaf2 multi-flag", "0:0:1")]:
    table = [correct_incorrect(m1, sub), correct_incorrect(m2, sub)]
    _, p, _, _ = chi2_contingency(table)
    print(f"{sub}: {m1} vs {m2}, chi-square P = {p:.2g}")
0:0:0: Assume unannotated is UP vs Leaf2 multi-flag, chi-square P = 4.3e-116
0:0:1: Leaf2 junction_classifier vs Leaf2 multi-flag, chi-square P = 5.4e-26
Code 
record_source("FigS4D", ref_d[["Method", "Subclass", "n_classified", "Accuracy"]])

Comprehensiveness of the annotation cannot fix what it fundamentally cannot see: the annotation-only methods are undefined or degenerate on 0:0:*, while both leafcutter2 methods still score there, and multi-flag’s consolidation over the bare junction_classifier flag is a significant improvement in both unannotated subclasses (both comparisons above, chi-square P < 1e-25).

Unannotated junctions: the case the annotation cannot reach

This is the panel that motivates the whole exercise. It restricts to completely unannotated junctions (0:0:0 and 0:0:1 pooled), against comprehensive Gencode, and asks how well leafcutter2’s own verdict recovers their productivity status.

An annotation-based method scores zero here by construction — it has nothing to say about a junction it has never seen. So the y-axis is not “is the classifier good”, it is “can anything be recovered at all”.

Each point is one (depth × bias) condition: colour is the fragment-bias condition, size is sequencing depth. The dashed diagonal is chance; the dotted line is the ceiling set by leafcutter2’s own abstentions.

Code 
BIAS_COLORS = {
    "alpha_1_beta_1": "#1b9e77",
    "alpha_1.5_beta_1": "#d95f02",
    "alpha_2.5_beta_1": "#7570b3",
    "alpha_4.5_beta_1": "#e7298a",
    "alpha_8.5_beta_1": "#66a61e",
}
BIAS_LABELS = {
    "alpha_1_beta_1": "Uniform coverage",
    "alpha_1.5_beta_1": "Slight 3' bias",
    "alpha_2.5_beta_1": "Moderate 3' bias",
    "alpha_4.5_beta_1": "Strong 3' bias",
    "alpha_8.5_beta_1": "Extreme 3' bias (low-RIN proxy)",
}
# Coverage_GB -> read pairs in millions, so the legend is in units people think in
COV_BREAKS = [0.3125, 0.625, 1.25, 2.5, 5, 10, 20]
COV_LABELS = ["1.56", "3.13", "6.25", "12.5", "25", "50", "100"]

# Pool the two unannotated subclasses, then recompute metrics on the pooled counts --
# these are ratios, so they cannot simply be averaged.
unannot = (
    metrics[metrics.Subclass.astype(str).isin(["0:0:0", "0:0:1"])]
    .groupby(["GTF", "Method", "Coverage_bias_Beta_params", "Coverage_GB"],
             dropna=False)[COUNT_COLS]
    .sum()
    .reset_index()
)
unannot["Recall_v2"] = unannot.TP / (
    unannot.TP + unannot.FN + unannot.UP_NE_ByMethod + unannot.UP_NotDetected)
unannot["FPR_v2"] = unannot.FP / (
    unannot.FP + unannot.TN + unannot.PR_NE_ByMethod + unannot.PR_NotDetected)

sr = unannot[
    unannot.GTF.eq("Comprehensive_Gencode")
    & unannot.Coverage_GB.notna()
    & unannot.Method.eq("Leaf2 multi-flag")
].copy()
# Order the factor so the legend reads uniform -> extreme; alphabetical would put
# alpha_1.5 before alpha_1.
sr["Coverage_bias_Beta_params"] = pd.Categorical(
    sr.Coverage_bias_Beta_params, categories=list(BIAS_COLORS), ordered=True)

# The ceiling is set by the junctions leafcutter2 returns NE for by design: those
# overlapping an annotated UTR, where its coding flag carries no information.
ref = unannot[
    unannot.GTF.eq("Comprehensive_Gencode")
    & unannot.Method.eq("Leaf2 multi-flag")
    & unannot.Coverage_GB.eq(20)
    & unannot.Coverage_bias_Beta_params.eq("alpha_1_beta_1")
].iloc[0]
n_up = ref.TP + ref.FN + ref.UP_NE_ByMethod + ref.UP_NotDetected
n_pr = ref.FP + ref.TN + ref.PR_NE_ByMethod + ref.PR_NotDetected
ceiling = 100 * (n_up - ref.UP_NE_ByMethod) / n_up

print(f"{int(n_up + n_pr):,} ground-truth labels in unannotated junctions "
      f"({100 * n_up / (n_up + n_pr):.1f}% unproductive)")
print(f"leafcutter2 returns NE for {int(ref.UP_NE_ByMethod):,} of {int(n_up):,} "
      f"unproductive ones -> recall ceiling {ceiling:.1f}%")

p_unannot = (
    ggplot(sr, aes("FPR_v2*100", "Recall_v2*100"))
    + geom_abline(slope=1, intercept=0, linetype="dashed", color="#b3b3b3", size=0.4)
    + geom_hline(yintercept=ceiling, linetype="dotted", color="#808080", size=0.5)
    + geom_point(aes(color="Coverage_bias_Beta_params", size="Coverage_GB"), alpha=0.9)
    + annotate(
        "text", x=2, y=ceiling - 3.5,
        label=f"{ceiling:.0f}% ceiling: leafcutter2 returns NE for UTR-overlapping junctions",
        ha="left", va="top", size=7, color="#666666")
    + scale_color_manual(values=BIAS_COLORS, labels=BIAS_LABELS,
                         name="Simulated coverage")
    + scale_size_continuous(name="Read pairs (M)", range=(1.2, 5),
                            breaks=COV_BREAKS, labels=COV_LABELS)
    + scale_x_continuous(breaks=[0, 25, 50, 75, 100])
    + scale_y_continuous(breaks=[0, 25, 50, 75, 100])
    + coord_cartesian(xlim=(0, 100), ylim=(0, 100))
    + labs(x="1 - Specificity (false-positive rate, %)", y="Recall (%)")

        legend_box="vertical",

record_source("Fig1F", sr[["Coverage_bias_Beta_params", "Coverage_GB", "FPR_v2", "Recall_v2"]])

Every point sits well above the diagonal, so unproductive junctions absent from every annotation are recoverable from short reads — the central claim. But the quantitative picture is worth stating precisely, because it is more modest than “recoverable” suggests:

  • Specificity is good, recall is partial. False-positive rate stays between 13% and 20%, while recall peaks at 61% — not at the 82% ceiling.
  • Recall saturates early. At uniform coverage it climbs 30% → 53% → 60% over the first three depth steps and then flattens: 5 GB gives 60.2% and 20 GB gives 60.9%. Past roughly 25 M read pairs, more sequencing buys essentially nothing.
  • Depth and 3’ bias matter about equally. Recall spans 30-61% across depths at uniform coverage, and 32-61% across bias conditions at full depth. Neither axis dominates.

Those two axes fail by the same mechanism, which the table makes visible: not misclassification but non-detection. UP_NotDetected accounts for 54% of unproductive junctions at the shallowest depth, and 53% at full depth under extreme 3’ bias. In both cases the junction is never observed, so no classifier could have called it.

That leaves the gap at the top. At 20 GB with uniform coverage only 0.2% of unproductive junctions go undetected, yet recall is 60.9% against an 82% ceiling — so about 21 points are genuine misclassification: junctions seen, called, and called productive when they are not. The remaining 18 points to 100% are leafcutter2’s abstentions, which it returns for junctions overlapping an annotated UTR because outside the CDS its coding flag carries no information about productivity. Recall_v2 charges those as misses, which is why they appear as a ceiling rather than being quietly excluded.

Does a more comprehensive annotation help?

Held at the best condition — 20 GB, uniform coverage — this crosses all four methods against all three annotation sets, for every subclass. Rows are metrics, columns are subclasses.

The question it answers: if a classifier is only as good as the annotation you give it, then moving from minimal (MANE) to comprehensive (Gencode) should lift performance across the board. It does not, and the bottom row shows why.

Code

    metrics[metrics.Coverage_GB.eq(20)
            & metrics.Coverage_bias_Beta_params.eq("alpha_1_beta_1")],
    metrics[metrics.Coverage_GB.isna()],
], ignore_index=True)

        sub.GTF.map(GTF_LABELS), categories=gtf_order, ordered=True)

                            values="Recall_v1") * 100,

        "Accuracy": sub.pivot(index="Method_long", columns="GTF_label",
                              values="Accuracy") * 100,
        "n": sub.pivot(index="Method_long", columns="GTF_label",
                       values="n_classified").astype(float),
    }
    for ridx, name in enumerate(metric_order):
        ax = axes[ridx, cidx]
        vals = mats[name].reindex(index=METHOD_LONG_LEVELS, columns=gtf_order).to_numpy()
        ax.imshow(np.ma.masked_invalid(vals),
                  cmap=perf_cmap if name != "n" else n_cmap,
                  norm=perf_norm if name != "n" else n_norm, aspect="auto")
        for i in range(vals.shape[0]):
            for j in range(vals.shape[1]):
                v = vals[i, j]
                if np.isnan(v):
                    lab = ""
                elif name == "n":
                    lab = f"{int(round(v)):,}"
                else:
                    lab = f"{v:.1f}"
                ax.text(j, i, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=4)
        ax.set_xticks(range(len(gtf_order)))
        ax.set_yticks(range(len(METHOD_LONG_LEVELS)))
        if ridx == len(metric_order) - 1:
            ax.set_xticklabels([g.replace("\n", " ") for g in gtf_order],
                               fontsize=5, rotation=35, ha="right")
        else:
            ax.set_xticklabels([])
        if cidx == 0:
            ax.set_yticklabels(METHOD_LONG_LEVELS, fontsize=5)
            ax.set_ylabel(name, fontsize=6)
        else:
            ax.set_yticklabels([])
        if ridx == 0:
            ax.set_title(subclass if subclass == "Overall"
                         else subclass.replace(":", "\n"), fontsize=6)
        for sp in ax.spines.values():
            sp.set_visible(True)
            sp.set_linewidth(0.4)
        ax.tick_params(length=0)

for row, cmap, cnorm, clabel in [
    (0, perf_cmap, perf_norm, "Performance metric (%)"),
    (-1, n_cmap, n_norm, "Number junctions classified"),
]:
    cax = inset_axes(axes[row, -1], width="8%", height="85%", loc="center left",
                     bbox_to_anchor=(1.08, 0.0, 1, 1),
                     bbox_transform=axes[row, -1].transAxes, borderpad=0)
    mpl.colorbar.ColorbarBase(
        cax, cmap=cmap, norm=cnorm, orientation="vertical").set_label(clabel, fontsize=6)

fig.supxlabel("Annotation source", fontsize=7)
fig.supylabel("Performance metric, classification approach", fontsize=7)
plt.show()

The 0:0:* columns are the point. There, the two annotation-only methods are blank or near-blank — an annotation cannot classify a junction it does not contain, however comprehensive — while both leafcutter2 readings still score. Comprehensiveness helps the annotation methods in the annotated subclasses, but it cannot manufacture coverage of the unannotated ones.

The bottom n row is the necessary companion: a high percentage over a handful of junctions is not the same claim as a high percentage over thousands, and reading the upper rows without it is how these comparisons get overstated.

Is the simulated coverage bias realistic?

A sanity check on the simulation itself, and the one figure here that does not come from the confusion table. If the Beta(alpha, 1) fragment-bias grid did not span the 3’ bias seen in real degraded RNA, the depth-and-bias axes above would not mean much.

Code 
def load_metagene(path):
    long = pd.read_csv(path, sep="\t").melt(
        id_vars="sample", var_name="bin", value_name="Coverage")
    long["bin"] = long["bin"].str.removeprefix("bin_").astype(int)
    long["Coverage"] = long.Coverage / long.groupby("sample").Coverage.transform("mean")
    return long

rin = load_metagene(OUTPUT / "Metagene" / "RIN_metagene_avg.txt")
sim = load_metagene(OUTPUT / "Metagene" / "Simulated_metagene_avg.txt")
meta = pd.read_csv(PROJECT / "code" / "config" / "RIN_Control_Samples.tsv", sep="\t")
rin = rin.merge(meta[["sample", "RIN"]], on="sample", how="left")
if rin.RIN.isna().any():
    raise ValueError(f"no RIN for: {sorted(rin.loc[rin.RIN.isna(), 'sample'].unique())}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(160 * MM, 120 * MM), sharex=True, sharey=True)

norm = mpl.colors.Normalize(vmin=rin.RIN.min(), vmax=rin.RIN.max())
for _, g in rin.groupby("sample"):
    g = g.sort_values("bin")
    axes[0].plot(g.bin, g.Coverage, lw=1.0, color=plt.cm.viridis(norm(g.RIN.iloc[0])))
axes[0].set_title("Real: short-read RNA-seq of degraded RNA", fontsize=9)
cb = fig.colorbar(mpl.cm.ScalarMappable(norm=norm, cmap=plt.cm.viridis),
                  ax=axes[0], pad=0.01, fraction=0.05)
cb.set_label("RIN", fontsize=8)
cb.ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)

for name, color in zip(BIAS_COLORS, plt.cm.Dark2.colors):
    g = sim[sim["sample"].eq(name)].sort_values("bin")
    if not g.empty:
        axes[1].plot(g.bin, g.Coverage, lw=1.3, color=color, label=BIAS_LABELS[name])
axes[1].set_title("Simulated: short reads from long-read cDNAs", fontsize=9)
axes[1].legend(fontsize=6.5, frameon=False, loc="upper left")

for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xticks([0, 100])
    ax.set_xticklabels(["TSS", "TES"], fontsize=8)
    ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=8)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
axes[1].set_xlabel("Relative position along transcript", fontsize=8)
fig.supylabel("Normalized coverage", fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The real libraries fan out with RIN: intact ones (yellow) are flat-to-5’-weighted, and the most degraded (dark purple, RIN 2) piles coverage at the 3’ end. The simulated grid reproduces that span, with alpha_8.5 reaching past the worst real sample. So the extreme end of the bias axis is not an extrapolation — it brackets real data.
